# Ti2p Core Level Analysis

The Ti2p core level was deconvoluted using four spin-orbit split doublets (eight components total) employing a mixed Lorentzian-Gaussian line shape model to account for the distinct chemical environments present in the titanium carbide sample. The TiC species was fitted with Lorentzian-Gaussian (LA) line shapes at binding energies of 454.80 eV (Ti2p3/2) and 460.80 eV (Ti2p1/2), with a constrained spin-orbit splitting of 5.85 eV and an area ratio of 0.50 reflecting the 2:1 intensity ratio expected for the 3/2:1/2 doublet. Three additional oxide phases were identified and fitted with symmetric Gaussian line shapes: TiO at 455.76 and 461.41 eV, Ti2O3 at 456.90 and 462.55 eV, and TiO2 at 458.28 and 464.05 eV, each with spin-orbit splittings constrained to 5.85 eV (or 5.72 eV for TiO2) and area ratios fixed at 0.50. The FWHM values for the 1/2 components were linked to scale with their corresponding 3/2 counterparts by a factor of approximately 1.9, ensuring physically reasonable peak widths across all species. The relative peak areas indicated that TiC dominated the surface composition (12,816 counts for Ti2p3/2), with oxide species comprising a substantially smaller fraction, suggesting either a thin surface oxidation layer or incomplete oxidation of the bulk titanium carbide material. These results are consistent with the expected surface chemistry of titanium carbide exposed to ambient conditions.

C1s.summary: The C1s core level spectrum was fitted with five singlet components using a Shirley background and a single Gaussian-Lorentzian line shape model. The dominant peak at 281.7 eV was assigned to titanium carbide (TiC), consistent with the expected binding energy for C atoms bonded to metal. The remaining components were attributed to adventitious carbon contamination: C–C/C–H at 284.6 eV, C–O at 285.9 eV, C=O at 286.6 eV, and O–C=O at 288.4 eV. The peak positions for the oxidized carbon species were constrained relative to the C–C reference component with fixed offsets of +1.2, +2.5, and +3.6 eV respectively, while the FWHM and Lorentzian-Gaussian ratio were held constant across all oxygenated species to reduce fitting degrees of freedom. The TiC carbide component dominated the spectrum with an area of 3649 counts, representing approximately 39% of the total fitted intensity, indicating that the sample surface retained substantial carbide character despite exposure to ambient conditions. The remaining 61% of the carbon signal arose from surface oxidation and hydrocarbon contamination, with the C–C species (5244 counts, 56%) being the most abundant contaminant phase, followed by minor contributions from C–O, C=O, and carboxylate functionalities (254, 194, and 207 counts respectively). This composition is typical of titanium carbide surfaces that have undergone partial oxidation and organic contamination during storage and handling.
